en: Kālidāsa: For the comprehension of both word and meaning, I salute Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, the parents of the world, who are joined together like word and meaning. (Raghuvamśa 1.1)
Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?
Out of delusion, I desire to cross the ocean that is so difficult to traverse by means of a mere raft.
"I am dull-witted yet seeking the fame of a poet; I shall become an object of ridicule, like a dwarf who, out of greed for a fruit reachable only by the tall, stretches out his arms."
Alternatively, since the gateway of speech has been opened for this lineage by former sages,
my way of entry is like that of a thread through a gem already perforated by a diamond.
Thus, [I shall describe] those kings who were pure from birth, whose actions bore fruit until their completion,
who ruled the earth as far as the ocean, and whose chariot tracks reached the very mines of the earth.

They had offered oblations into the sacred fires according to the prescribed rites; they honored supplicants with gifts according to their desires; they meted out punishments according to the nature of the offense; and they remained awake at their appointed times.
For those who have accumulated wealth for the sake of giving; for those who speak measuredly for the sake of truth;
for those desiring victory for the sake of fame; and for householders for the sake of progeny.
Having mastered the sciences in childhood, seeking the objects of the senses in youth,
adopting the conduct of sages in old age, and finally casting off the body through yoga at the end.
Though my power of speech is meager, I shall describe the lineage of the Raghus,
having been deceived into this rashness by their virtues which have entered my ears.
The virtuous, who are the means of discerning the real from the unreal, ought to listen to this;
for the purity or the impurity of gold is perceived in the fire.
There was one named Manu, the son of Vivasvat, who was honored by the wise as the first among the rulers of the earth, just as the syllable *praṇava* is among the Vedic meters.
In that pure lineage was born an even purer one,
Dilīpa by name, like a moon among kings, as the moon is born from the ocean of milk.
Broad-chested, with shoulders like those of a bull, tall as a *sāla* tree, and long-armed,
he possessed a body suited to his own deeds, as if he were the very dharma of the warrior class incarnate.
With his essence surpassing all others, eclipsing all splendor,
and standing as the highest of all, he traversed the earth with his person like Mount Meru.
His wisdom was commensurate with his appearance; his sacred learning was commensurate with his wisdom;
his undertakings were commensurate with his learning; and his success was commensurate with his undertakings.
By means of his royal qualities, which were both formidable and attractive,
he was both unassailable and approachable to his dependents, just as the ocean is both unapproachable and accessible due to its aquatic gems.

Not even by so much as the breadth of a line did his subjects ever deviate from the path of their own selves, which had been trodden by him; they moved like the revolutions of the wheel-rims under the control of a driver.
For the sake of the prosperity of his subjects alone, he accepted tribute from them;
for the sun draws up moisture only to release it back a thousandfold.
His army and his equipment were his two means for accomplishing his goals:
his intellect was engaged in the study of the scriptures, and his bowstring was drawn upon his bow.
The undertakings of that king, who kept his counsel secret and concealed his outward gestures and internal intentions,
could only be inferred from their results, like the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous life.
Fearless, he protected himself; free from illness, he practiced dharma;
without greed, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness.
Silence in the face of knowledge, forbearance in the face of power, and the absence of self-praise in the face of renunciation—
these virtues of his seemed as if they were siblings, for they were bound together by their common quality.
Unattracted by sense objects, having reached the further shore of the sciences,
and delighting in dharma, he attained old age without the physical decay of senility.
Because he disciplines, instructs, protects, and sustains his subjects, he is their father;
their biological fathers are merely the cause of their birth.

For that wise king, even the pursuit of wealth and pleasure was rooted solely in righteousness: in punishing those deserving of punishment for the sake of stability, and in marriage for the sake of progeny.
That Maghavan milked the earth for sacrifice and the heavens for grain;
through the exchange of their respective riches, the two of them sustained both worlds.
Indeed, no other kings ever equaled the fame of that protector;
for while he had turned away from the property of others, the practice of thievery remained confined to the Vedas.
Even if he was disliked, the disciplined man was esteemed by him as a sick man values medicine;
yet even a beloved person, if wicked, was to be abandoned like a finger bitten by a snake.
Surely the Creator fashioned him through the meditative absorption of the great elements;
for indeed, all his qualities had as their sole fruit the welfare of others.
He ruled the earth— encircled by the ocean as its moat and bounded by the coastal ranges—
as if it were a single city, under his undisputed command.
His wife, born of the Magadha lineage, was named Sudakṣiṇā— a name rooted in his own courtesy— and she was like the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of a ritual.

The lord of the earth considered himself possessed of a wife by virtue of that high-minded lady, even though he already had a large harem, just as one considers oneself possessed of a wife through the goddess Lakṣmī.
Eager for the birth of a son from her who was worthy of himself,
he passed his time with desires whose fulfillment was long delayed.
Just as Bhagīratha entrusted the Gaṅgā— capable of purifying his ancestors—
to others when he desired offspring, so did he entrust Kosala to his ministers.
Then, having worshipped the Creator with self-restraint out of a desire for a son,
the couple went to the hermitage of their preceptor Vasiṣṭha.
They mounted a single chariot that emitted a smooth and deep resonance,
like lightning and Airāvata upon a rain-cloud of the monsoon season.
Lest there be any disturbance to the hermitage, they were preceded by a limited number of attendants,
like an elephant and his mate followed by a small herd of scent-elephants and young calves.
They were served by breezes pleasant to the touch, fragrant with the resin of the *sāla* tree,
scattering the pollen of flowers, and shaking the rows of forest trees.
Because the wind was favorable, foretelling the fulfillment of their prayers,
the dust kicked up by the horses did not touch the curls of their hair or the veils of their garments.
Taking fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*), they approached the elders of the cowherd settlements and inquired about the names of the wild trees along the path.
In the lakes, they inhaled the fragrance of the lotuses, cooled by the agitation of the waves and resembling their own breath.
Delighting their minds, they listened as the peacocks, with heads turned toward the sound of the chariot wheels,
uttered cries divided into two tones that harmonized with the *ṣaḍja* note.
They gazed at pairs of deer whose eyes resembled one another's, which had left the path not far behind, as their own eyes were fixed upon the chariot.
In some places, with their faces raised by cranes whose sweet cries formed, as it were, a pillarless archway-garland through their continuous rows; Ragh(K) 1.44.
In the villages established by themselves and marked by sacrificial posts, they received,
at every step, unfailing blessings from the sacrificers as they accepted the offerings of honor.

As those two, dressed in pure white garments, proceeded together, they possessed a certain indescribable splendor, like the conjunction of the moon with the constellation Citrā when freed from the clouds of winter.
Pointing out various lords of the land to his wife, the handsome prince,
who was like a wise Buddha, did not even perceive that the journey had been traversed.
Having attained a fame difficult to acquire, he reached the hermitage in the evening with his weary mount,
accompanied by the queen of that great seer who was self-restrained.
It was being filled with ascetics who had returned from the depths of the forest, carrying fuel-sticks and kusha grass suspended from their shoulders,
and rendered pure by rising to meet the sacred fires.

At the edge of the watering-place, where the trees had been cleared away by the daughters of sages for the sake of providing water to the basins from which the birds might drink to their heart's content;
In the courtyards of the leaf-huts, where wild rice had been gathered as the heat of the sun subsided,
deer sat and performed the act of chewing the cud.
It was crowded with deer, accustomed to receiving their share of wild rice, who blocked the doors of the hermits’ huts as if they were their own offspring.
He was purifying the hermitage with smoke wafted by the wind— smoke that bore the fragrance of oblations and was heralded by the fires being kindled for guests approaching the retreat.
Then, having instructed the charioteer to let the draft animals rest,
he helped his wife descend from the chariot and descended himself.
To him, the protector who was accompanied by his wife, those sages— whose senses were most well-guarded— offered worship due to one worthy of honor, for he possessed the eye of political wisdom.
At the conclusion of his evening rites, he beheld that treasure-house of asceticism seated beside Arundhatī,
like the consumer of oblations (Agni) beside Svāhā.
The King and the Queen of Magadha grasped their feet;
as preceptor and preceptor’s wife, they greeted them with affection.
The hospitable sage questioned that sage of the royal order about his welfare in the kingdom, as he had been relieved of the fatigue of the journey by the hospitality shown to him.
Then, in the presence of that Atharvanic treasure whose cities of enemies had been conquered,
the Lord of Wealth, the best among speakers, took up words full of meaning.
Is it not indeed fitting that prosperity has come to me, whose seven limbs you are the dispeller of both divine and human calamities?
By your mantras, which restrain enemies from afar,
my arrows— though they pierce their visible targets— are as it were repelled.
O Hotṛ priest, the oblation offered by you according to the prescribed rites into the fires becomes rain for the crops that have been withered by drought.
That my subjects live for a full human lifespan, free from disease and calamities, is due to the spiritual luster of your Brahmanic power.
Thus, as I am being instructed by my preceptor, the source of the Veda,
how could my prosperity not be free from calamity and accompanied by its proper consequences?
But since this daughter-in-law of yours has not yet borne a child worthy of her,
even the earth— with its islands and its yield of jewels— does not satisfy me.
Surely, perceiving that it is difficult to find anyone superior to me,
my ancestors now enjoy the water I have offered, which has been warmed by their own sighs.
Thus, with my soul purified by sacrifice yet obscured by the failure of progeny,
I am like the mountain Lokāloka— both light and darkness.
Merit arising from austerity and charity brings happiness in other worlds;
however, a lineage of pure descent leads to well-being both in this world and the next.
How is it that the Teacher, beholding me bereft of her, does not feel pain,
as if looking upon a sapling in the hermitage that he himself had watered with affection, yet now stands barren?
"O Blessed One, know that this bond of debt causes me unbearable pain,
like a goad that wounds the tender flesh of a newly captured elephant."
Therefore, you ought to provide such arrangements that I may be liberated;
for even in matters difficult to achieve for the Ikṣvākus, success depends entirely upon you.
Thus addressed by the king, the sage, his eyes motionless in meditation,
remained for a moment like a lake whose fish are asleep.
Then he, whose soul was purified through meditation, perceived by means of his vow the cause of the obstruction to the lineage; thereupon, he enlightened the Lord of the Earth regarding this matter.
Formerly, as you were returning to the earth after attending upon Śakra,
Surabhi was found by you on the road, resting in the shade of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
Having remembered this queen after her ritual bath at the end of her menses, he immediately and hastily bypassed the rite of circumambulation, thereby provoking her anger.
"Since you despise me,
you shall have no offspring without having propitiated my progeny"— thus did she curse him.
O King, that curse was heard neither by you nor by the charioteer,
as the celestial Gaṅgā roared with its current amidst the wild elephants of the quarters.
I understand that my desire depends on his favor;
for the neglect of honoring those worthy of worship obstructs one's spiritual welfare.
That [sacrificial ground] of the wise one, intended for the oblation of a long-duration sacrifice,
now stands over Pātāla, its entrance blocked by serpents.
Therefore, together with your wife, propitiate her who is the mother of my calf and stands one degree lower than her; she will grant you both your desire.
Even as the Hotṛ priest was speaking thus,
a blameless cow named Nandinī, the means for his sacrificial oblation, returned from the forest.
Bearing a coppery line upon her forehead that was darker than the rest,
she resembled the twilight mingled with the new moon.
The cow with full udders showered the earth with her warm, pure milk, even more sanctifying than the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*),
as it flowed forth at the sight of her calf.
By the particles of dust raised by their hooves that touched his body from close at hand,
the king received the purity born of bathing in sacred waters.
Having seen her, whose appearance was auspicious, the ascetic who knew omens spoke again to his patron, whose prayer had now been proven fruitful: "Ragh(K)_1.85 //"
O King, consider that success is not far off for you,
since this auspicious lady has appeared as soon as her name was uttered.
Subsisting on forest fare, you ought to propitiate this cow by constantly following her, just as one seeks to master knowledge through constant practice.
When she has set out, you should set out; when she has stopped, you should take up your station;
when she is seated, you should sit down; and when she has drunk water, you should drink water.
And let the devoted daughter-in-law follow her as she departs for the penance grove after being honored,
in the morning, and likewise go out to meet her in the evening.
Until she is pleased, remain devoted to her service;
may you be free from obstacles, and may you stand at the head of those who have sons, like a father.
"So be it," replied the disciple, full of joy and accompanied by his retinue; knowing the proper time and place, he, bowing low before his teacher, accepted the command of his instructor.

Then, at twilight, the son of the Creator, who knew the faults [of the world] and spoke with pleasant truth, dismissed the lord of the people, who possessed formidable splendor, for the sake of retiring to rest.
Although he possessed perfection in asceticism, the sage,
who was skilled in ritual procedures, ordained for him a forest dwelling that was consistent with his religious observances.
Having occupied the leaf-hut pointed out by the head of the family,
accompanied by his devoted wife as his only companion, he spent the night lying on a bed of *kuśa* grass, its end signaled by the recitation of his pupil.
Thus ends the first canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.

Then at dawn, the lord of subjects, whose wealth was his fame, released for the forest the sage’s cow, from which he had accepted perfumes and garlands as a gift from his wife, and whose calf had been tied up after drinking its fill.

The lawful wife of the lord of men, who was herself free from worldly dust, followed her path— whose dust was purified by the placement of her husband's hooves— just as the Smṛti follows the meaning of the Śruti.
Having turned back his beloved wife, the compassionate king— fragrant with fame— protected that daughter of Surabhi,
who had become like the earth itself assuming the form of a cow, with the four oceans serving as her udders.
For the sake of his vow, he prohibited even the rest of his retinue from following the cow;
for his protection of the body did not depend on others, as the progeny of Manu is guarded by its own prowess.
With mouthfuls of grass that were full of flavor, by scratching her to relieve her itching, by warding off gadflies,
and by allowing her unhindered freedom of movement, the Emperor became entirely intent on her service.
Standing when she stood, moving when she moved, sitting firm upon his seat when she sat down,
and desiring water when she took water, the king followed her like a shadow.

Bearing royal fortune even though its outward signs had been laid aside— fortune inferred only by his extraordinary majesty— he remained like a lordly elephant in a state of internal rut, whose flow of ichor was not yet manifest.
With his hair entwined by the spreading tendrils of creepers, he roamed the forest with his bow strung,
as if intending to discipline the wild beasts under the pretext of guarding the sacrificial cow of his preceptor.

As he had dismissed his attendants from his side, the trees by his side, as if equal to Varuṇa the wielder of the noose, seemed to utter the cries of "Look! through the warbling of birds intoxicated with joy.

And young creepers, impelled by the Maruts, showered flowers upon him— who resembled a friend of the Maruts and was worthy of worship— as he approached from nearby, just as city maidens scatter parched grain in accordance with custom.
Even though he was a wielder of the bow, the deer-eyed women, their hearts having been told of his compassionate nature by their own unhesitating inner selves,
beheld his form and attained the full fruit of the wide expansion of their eyes.
In the groves, he heard his own fame being loudly sung by the forest deities, while the bamboos, their hollows filled with the wind, produced the effect of a flute as they whistled.
The wind, mingled with the spray of forest waterfalls and fragrant with the scent of flowers shaken from the trees,
attended upon him— who was purified by his conduct, who lacked a parasol, and who was weary from the heat of the sun.
Even without rain, the forest fire was extinguished; there was an extraordinary increase in fruits and flowers;
and while he entered that forest as its protector, no one among the creatures was oppressed by another.
Having purified the quarters of the sky with its wanderings, at the close of day,
the radiance of the sun— copper-red like the hue of a young sprout— and the cow of the sage both set out to return to their respective abodes.
The protector of the middle world followed her for the sake of performing rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests;
accompanied by him, who was esteemed by the virtuous, she became like Faith herself visibly manifested through the prescribed ritual.

He proceeded, beholding forests turning dark green, where herds of boars had emerged from the ponds, where peacocks looked up toward the trees that served as their dwellings, and where the young grass was inhabited by deer.
The young cow, from the effort of bearing the weight of her full udders, and the king, from the heaviness of his chest,
both graced the path on their return from the penance grove with their elegant gaits.
As he was returning from the edge of the forest following Vasiṣṭha’s cow, his wife drank him in with her eyes—
whose lashes were slow to blink— as if they had been fasting.
Honored on the path by the king and welcomed by the king’s lawful wife,
that cow shone between them like the twilight between day and night.
Having circumambulated that milch-cow, Sudakṣiṇā, with a vessel of parched grain in her hand,
bowed down and worshipped its broad space between the horns as if it were the gateway to her own spiritual perfection.

Although she was anxious for her calf, she received the ritual offerings with composure; thus the two of them rejoiced, for among those endowed with devotion, the signs of grace from such beings are indeed the precursors of the fruit.
Having pressed the feet of his preceptor together with his wife and having completed the evening rites, Dilīpa—
by whom his enemies had been destroyed by the strength of his arms— again attended upon the milch-cow as she sat down after the conclusion of her milking.

Having attended to her as she sat by the offerings and lamps placed nearby, the protector, accompanied by his wife, lay down after she had gradually fallen asleep; and in the morning, he rose after she had awakened from sleep.
Thus, as he of exalted fame— who was ever fit for uprooting his enemies— observed this vow for the sake of his subjects together with his queen,
seven times three days passed by.
On another day, the sage’s sacrificial cow, desiring to ascertain the disposition of her follower,
entered a cave of the mountain of Gaurī where young grass grew at the edge of the fall of the Gaṅgā.

It is said that a lion, whose eyes were fixed upon the beauty of the mountain, suddenly seized her by force; for she was unassailable even in thought by predatory beasts, and the king did not notice his springing forward.

The king’s gaze, which the lord of mountains had granted him like a ray of light, was drawn back by the cry of that distressed sage— a cry made long by its echo within the cave— as if it had seized it with its own beams.
That archer beheld a lion standing upon a pale-red cow,
like a blossoming *rodhra* tree on a mountain ridge atop a mineral-rich plateau.

Then the king, who moved like the lord of beasts, who was a refuge for those seeking protection, and who had forcibly uprooted his enemies, drew an arrow from his quiver with the intent to slay that beast which deserved death.
The other hand of that archer,
with its fingers still clinging to the feathered end of the arrow whose shaft was stained by the luster of his nails, remained as if its movement were fixed in a painting.
His anger increased by the obstruction of his arms as he could not touch the offender who stood so near,
the king burned within himself with his own majesty, like a serpent whose power is neutralized by a mantra.
Having restrained his cow, the lion— whose lineage was noble, who was the banner of Manu’s race,
and who was a lion among kings— addressed that king in human speech, causing him amazement at his own mastery of the art of illusion.
Enough of your exertion, O protector of the earth; even a weapon discharged here would be in vain.
The force of the wind, though capable of uprooting trees, does not prevail against a mountain peak.

Know me to be Kumbhodara by name, a friend of Nikumbha and a servant of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), whose back has been purified by the grace of the imprint of His foot as He desired to mount His bull, white as Mount Kailāsa.
Do you see yonder Devadāru tree before you? This tree was adopted as a son by the bull-bannered Lord Śiva;
it is the one that knows the taste of the milk flowing from the golden-pot breasts of Skanda’s mother.
Once, while scratching his flank, the skin of this [elephant] was torn away by a wild elephant;
then the daughter of the Mountain grieved for him, as if for a general pierced by the weapons of the Asuras.

From that time forth, the wielder of the trident, having assumed the form of a lion whose livelihood consists in preying upon creatures that come into his clutches, appointed me to this mountain valley for the purpose of terrifying elephants.
This [offering], ordained by the Supreme Lord at the appointed time, is sufficient for the satiation of that hungry one;
it has arrived as my feast of blood, just as the nectar of the moon is for the enemy of the gods.
Therefore, casting aside shame, you should return; for you have demonstrated devotion to your preceptor.
That which is to be protected by a weapon but cannot be protected does not diminish the fame of those who bear arms.
Having heard these bold words of the king of beasts, the lord of men,
his weapons rendered ineffective by the power of Śiva, relaxed the self-contempt he had felt toward himself.
And he replied to him regarding the discharge of the arrow during that first encounter, his effort rendered futile,
like the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) wishing to release his vajra when he has been paralyzed by the gaze of Tryambaka (Śiva).
O Lord of Beasts, the words I wish to speak may well seem laughable to one whose movements are thus restrained;
yet you know every internal state of living beings, and therefore I shall speak.
He is venerable to me as the cause of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of all things mobile and immobile;
furthermore, this wealth of my preceptor, who maintains the sacred fires, must not be neglected while it is perishing before our eyes.
Therefore, be gracious and sustain your bodily existence with my own body;
O Great Sage, let this cow, who is anxious for her young calf at the close of day, be released.
Then, shattering the darkness of the mountain caves with the rays of his fangs,
that attendant of the Lord of Beings once more smiled slightly and spoke to Arthapati.
Sovereignty over the world under a single umbrella, fresh youth, and this lovely body—
you, wishing to abandon so much for the sake of a trifle, appear to me to be deluded by a lack of discernment.
If you have compassion for living beings, then at the end of your life this single cow shall be well;
furthermore, O Lord of Subjects, while living, you shall always protect your people from calamities like a father.
Now, you fear the punishment for the offense against the single cow from your preceptor, who is like a mere plowman;
yet his wrath can be appeased by you by presenting him with crores of cows with udders as large as jars.
Therefore, protect your own vigorous body, which is the enjoyer of a succession of auspicious blessings;
for they say that a prosperous kingdom is no different from the status of Indra himself, save for its mere contact with the surface of the earth.
When the lord of beasts had ceased after saying this much, the mountain peak, through its echo returning from the caves,
seemed to address that very same matter loudly to the protector of the earth out of affection.
To the attendant of the gods who had spoken such capable words, Dilīpa replied,
looking even more deeply moved by compassion as he was gazed upon by the cow, whose eyes were timid at being sat upon.
The exalted word *kṣatra*, well-established throughout the worlds, is indeed derived from the notion that it "protects from injury" (*kṣatāt trāyate*).
Of what use is sovereignty, or life itself, stained by reproach, to one whose conduct is the opposite of that?
And how could it be possible for the Great Sage to show favor by bestowing other milk-yielding cows?
Know this: she is no less than Surabhi herself; you have struck her down by the power of Rudra.
Therefore, it is right for me to release you from him by paying the ransom of my own body;
in this way, your breaking of the fast will not be frustrated, and the purpose of the Sage’s ritual act will remain unimpaired.
Your Honor also understands this from the words of others, for great indeed is your effort toward the Devadāru tree;
yet it is possible for a protector to stand before his charge and destroy what must be protected himself, remaining unhurt.
If you consider me someone who must not be harmed, then show compassion for my body of fame;
for those like me have indeed no regard for material bodies, which are destined for absolute destruction.
They say that a relationship is preceded by conversation; such a bond was formed between us when we met at the edge of the forest.
Therefore, O follower of the Lord of Beings, you ought not to reject the request of one who is your kinsman.
Saying "So be it" to the cow, Dilīpa immediately released his arm from its paralysis;
having laid down his weapons, he offered his own body to Hari as if it were a morsel of meat.
At that moment, as the protector of his subjects was looking on with a fierce lion-leap,
a rain of flowers released from the hands of the Vidyādharas fell upon him as he stood with his face turned downward.
Having heard these words, which were like nectar, "Arise, my child," he rose up;
and having risen, the king beheld before him his own cow, dripping with milk as if she were his mother, and not the lion.
To him who was thus amazed, the cow said: "O virtuous one, you have been tested by me through the manifestation of an illusion.
By the power of the seer, even Death himself is not able to strike me, much less other predatory beasts."
"O son, I am pleased with you because of your devotion to your guru and your compassion for me; choose a boon.
Know that I, the wish-fulfilling cow, being well-disposed, am not merely the source of milk."
Then, having summoned him, he who honored his supplicants and had earned for himself the title of "Hero" by his own hand,
requested from Sudakṣiṇā a son who would be the founder of his lineage and possess infinite fame.
Having promised the king, who desired progeny, that his wish would be granted, that milch-cow milked her own milk into a leaf-cup and instructed him, "My son, drink this."
O Mother, having obtained the sage’s permission for the remainder of the calf after the rules for the fire-oblation have been fulfilled,
I wish to enjoy your milk, just as one enjoys the sixth part of the earth when it has been protected.
Thus addressed by the lord of the earth, Vasiṣṭha’s cow became exceedingly pleased;
accompanied by him, she returned from the slopes of the Himalayas to the hermitage as if without any fatigue.
The preceptor of kings, his moon-like face radiant with serenity, having communicated his favor to the Guru,
declared it to his beloved once again through words that were a mere repetition of what was already evident from the serenity of his countenance.

Having received permission from Vasiṣṭha, that man of blameless soul, who was ever affectionate toward his subjects, drank the milk of Nandinī— the residue remaining after her calf had drunk— which was as pure as fame itself, and he remained insatiable, as if drinking it for the first time.
At dawn, at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast as prescribed by his vow,
the self-controlled Vasiṣṭha performed the auspicious rite for departure and sent the royal couple back toward their own capital.
Having circumambulated the fire into which oblations had been offered, and then his husband, Arundhatī,
and a cow with her calf, the king set forth, his majesty further intensified by these auspicious omens.
Accompanied by his lawful wife, the patient king traveled along a road pleasant for its lack of jolting, drawn by a chariot whose sound was pleasing to the ear, as if by his own fulfilled desire.
The subjects, their longing aroused by his absence and their bodies emaciated by vows for the sake of progeny,
drank him in with eyes that could not reach satiety, as if he were the newly risen lord of medicinal herbs.
Having entered the city, which was adorned with raised banners, Purandaraśrī was greeted with joy by the citizens;
he once again took up the burden of the earth upon his arm, which possessed strength equal to that of the lord of serpents.
Then, as the sky receives the light arising from the eyes of Atri, or as the celestial river receives the splendor of Śiva discharged by fire,
the queen conceived a fetus for the prosperity of the royal lineage— a fetus infused with the weighty majesties of the world-protectors.
Thus ends the second canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.

Then Sudakṣiṇā bore the signs of pregnancy— the very omen of the continuity of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, the fulfillment of her husband’s desire, and the moonlight-like face of her friends’ joyful glances— at the dawning of its fulfillment.
With her face as pale as a ketaka petal, her slender body, and her few ornaments, she,
with her delicate form, imitated the night at dawn when the moon’s orb has grown faint and only a few stars remain.
Having smelled that face, which was stained with earth, the king found no satisfaction,
just as an elephant finds no satiety at a pond in a forest grove sprinkled by the drops of clouds at the end of the hot season.
"For my son shall enjoy the earth as Indra enjoys heaven, for his chariot will rest only at the ends of the quarters;
therefore, disregarding other pleasures, she first fixed her mind upon such a desire. (Raghuvamśa 3.4)
"Out of modesty, the Magadhan princess does not tell me anything she desires; in what things does she have longing?
Thus the Lord of Uttarakosala, full of respect, would frequently ask his beloved's female companions.
Having approached her state of longing due to pregnancy-cravings, whatever she chose, that very thing she saw brought before her;
for there was nothing desired by her that was difficult to obtain even in heaven for the king, once he had strung his bow.
As the days passed, her two breasts, pale as madhūka flowers with dark nipples at their tips,
bore the luster of two ivory caskets covered with sheaths of black buffalo horn.
Having gradually overcome the discomfort of her pregnancy longings, she shone with the full development of her limbs, like a creeper that,
immediately upon the falling away of its old leaves, is adorned with beautiful new sprouts.

The king regarded his queen as pregnant, like the ocean-clad earth containing hidden treasures, like a *śamī* tree with fire concealed within, and like the river Sarasvatī with its waters flowing inside.

That steadfast king performed the *puṃsavana* and other rites in due order— rites appropriate for his passion for his beloved, the exaltation of his mind, the wealth acquired by his arms from the ends of the earth, and his own fortitude.

The king rejoiced when she entered the house, her body heavy with the burden of the womb resting upon the lap of Surendramātṛ; she had risen from her seat with effort, her hands were weary from the gesture of respectful salutation, and her eyes were tremulous.
Then, attended by skilled physicians and trusted pediatricians within the lying-in chamber,
she shone as she remained there for a safe delivery, like a ritual action whose fruit is imminent.

Then, at the auspicious time, Trishāḍhanā, who was like Śacī, gave birth to a son whose abundant fortune was indicated by five planets situated in their exaltations and not conjoined with the Sun— just as the power of the three means (of virtue, wealth, and pleasure) brings forth unimpaired prosperity.
The quarters became serene, the winds blew auspiciously, and the sacrificial fire accepted the oblation with its flames turning to the right;
at that moment, everything portended good fortune, for such is the nature of the birth of those destined for the exaltation of the world.
By the innate splendor of that noble-born one, which spread all around his deathbed,
the midnight lamps were suddenly robbed of their luster and became as if fixed in a painting.

To the person of the inner apartments who announced the birth of the prince in words as sweet as nectar, there were only three things that the king could not give: the moon-bright parasol and the two fly-whisks.

Beholding his son’s face after so long a time— like a destitute man seeing a jar of buried treasure— the father was so overcome with joy that he could no longer contain himself within his own body, just as the ocean swells at the rising of the moon.
When the entire birth-rite had been performed by the ascetic family priest who had come from the penance grove,
the son of Dilīpa shone with even greater luster, like a gem risen from its mine that has undergone the proper refinement.
The sounds of auspicious musical instruments, pleasant to hear, accompanied by the joyful dances of courtesans,
resounded not only within the palace of the Lord of Magadha, but also along the path of the gods.
There was no one whom that protector, delighted by the birth of a son, would have released from confinement;
yet at that time, he himself alone was liberated from the bondage of his ancestors known as "debt."
Considering that this child would reach the end of what has been heard, as well as the ends of enemies in battle, the king,
who understood the meaning of words, gave his own offspring the name Raghu, for the root *ragh* signifies "to go."
Through his father’s efforts and through all manner of auspicious blessings, he grew day by day with every limb of his body becoming more beautiful,
like the young moon waxing as it enters the rays of the sun.
Just as Umā and the Bull-bannered Lord [Śiva] rejoice with Śarajanman [Kārttikeya], and as Śacī and Purandara [Indra] rejoice with Jayanta,
so did the King and the Magadhan princess, who were their equals, rejoice with their son who resembled them.
The mutual bond of affection between the two, who were like the two wheels of a chariot,
did not diminish toward one another even though it was divided by their single son.
When that child spoke the first words uttered by his nurse, when he walked while grasping her finger,
and when he became humble through the instruction of prostration— he thereby spread great joy for his father.
Having placed him upon his lap, the king— his eyes half-closed— gradually attained the savor of the touch of his son, as if drenching his skin with nectar born from the contact of their bodies.

And he, the preserver of the world, considered his own lineage— endowed with stability— to have been elevated by this man of supreme birth, just as the Lord of Creatures considers his own creation to be perfected through the manifestation of his own form acting through the preeminent qualities.
With his topknot trimmed and accompanied by sons of ministers of his own age who wore dangling side-locks of hair,
he entered the ocean of literature through the proper mastery of writing, as one enters the sea by way of a river mouth.
Then the wise teachers, who were dear to their preceptor, instructed him according to the prescribed rules once he had been initiated;
and their efforts there became fruitful, for an action directed toward a worthy object indeed bears fruit.
That noble-minded one, through his complete virtues, gradually crossed over the four branches of learning— which are like the four oceans—
just as the Lord of the Monkeys traversed the quarters with his bay horses that outstripped the wind.
Having donned the sacred skin of the Ruru deer, he practiced the use of missiles under his father’s guidance according to the sacred mantras;
thus, he became the foremost knower of the secrets of both the discharge and withdrawal of weapons, just like Purandara.
Like a young calf attaining the state of a great bull, or like a young elephant reaching the condition of a lordly tusker,
Raghu— his childhood gradually supplanted by youth— cultivated a body that was both profound and enchanting.
Then, immediately after the rite of the cutting of the hair (godāna), the Lord performed his initiation for marriage;
having obtained him as a virtuous husband, the daughters of the king shone like the daughters of Dakṣa who had attained the Sun, the dispeller of darkness.

A youth with arms as long as a yoke, muscular, with a chest like a door-panel and a well-rounded neck, Raghu surpassed his elder in excellence of physique; nevertheless, he appeared humble through his modesty.

Then, perceiving through the eye of his intellect that his son was self-controlled, the king— intending to lighten the exceedingly heavy burden of the subjects which he had long borne himself— conferred upon him the title of crown prince.

Then Fortune, desiring his virtues, departed from the primary abode of the king for that residence known as the crown prince; she went there in part, just as she moves from a lotus to a newly blossomed water-lily.
Like the sun at dawn with the wind as its charioteer, or like the sun at the end of the rainy season with its rays fully manifest,
the king became exceedingly difficult to withstand because of him, just as an elephant becomes irresistible when its temples are bursting with rut.
Having appointed him to guard the sacrificial horse, followed by princes who were archers, he—
equal to Indra— completed his hundred sacrifices without obstacle, lacking only one.
After this,

Śakra, it is said, assuming a concealed form, seized the horse that had been released without restraint for the sacrifice by that sacrificer, right before the eyes of the archers who were its guardians.
Then the prince’s army stood still, struck with wonder and its resolve lost in despondency;
at that moment, Nandini, the cow of Vasiṣṭha, whose power was well known, appeared there by chance.
Then, having wiped his eyes with a meritorious drop of the fluid flowing from that [ointment],
the son of Dilīpa became one whose vision was attained even regarding objects beyond the senses, as he was held in high esteem by the virtuous.
Born from a king of men, he beheld on the east that god who shatters the wings of mountains,
repeatedly restraining the horse’s restlessness as urged by the charioteer, while the horse was held fast by the reins of the chariot.
Recognizing Hari by his hundreds of unblinking eyes and by his tawny horses,
Raghu addressed him in a deep voice that touched the heavens, as if calling him back.
O Lord of the Gods, since you alone are declared by the wise to be the foremost among those who partake in the sacrificial portions,
how can you proceed to obstruct the ritual of my preceptor, who is engaged in perpetual consecration?
As the Lord of the Three Worlds, you who possess divine vision must surely restrain the enemies of sacrifice;
yet if you yourself become an obstacle to the deeds of those practicing dharma, the sacred law has fallen into ruin.
Therefore, O Maghavan, you ought to release this horse, the foremost limb of the great sacrifice;
for lords who show the pure path do not adopt a defiled track.
Having heard these bold words uttered by Raghu, the lord of the gods,
filled with wonder, turned his chariot back and proceeded to offer a reply.
O prince, it is exactly as you have said; glory must be protected on all sides by those for whom glory is their wealth.
Yet your father is now intent upon surpassing that entire world-renowned fame through his sacrifice.
Just as Hari alone is remembered as Puruṣottama, and Maheśvara alone, the three-eyed one, and no other;
so do the sages know me, Śatakratu—for this title of ours does not apply to a second person.
Therefore, this horse was carried off by me from your father while he was imitating Kapila;
enough of this effort on your part—do not set foot upon the path of Sagara’s progeny.
Then, free from fear, the son of the Indra of the earth laughed and spoke again to Purandara:
"Take up your weapon if this is your resolve; for you shall certainly not achieve your purpose without first conquering Raghu."
Having spoken thus to Maghavan, he stood with his face turned upward, about to take up his bow along with an arrow;
by the excellence of his physical form, which was graced by the *ālīḍha* posture, he emulated the Lord [Śiva] himself.
Wounded in the heart by Raghu’s arrow— which was composed of sheer audacity— even the impatient Indra,
the breaker of mountains, fixed an unerring shaft upon his bow at the moment marked by the appearance of a fresh bank of clouds.
Having entered the broad chest of the prince, that swift arrow— accustomed to the blood of fearsome demons—
fell upon human blood as if out of curiosity, for it had never tasted such before.

The prince of Hari, too, possessing the prowess of a youth, fixed an arrow bearing his own name upon the arm of Indra— the arm that was hardened by the lashing of the celestial elephant's trunk and marked with the decorative patterns of Śacī’s leaf-designs.
And with another arrow marked by a peacock feather, he struck down Indra’s great thunderbolt-bannered standard;
the king of the gods grew violently incensed at him, as if his very hair had been forcibly shorn from his divine splendor.

Between those two, who were both desirous of victory, there occurred a tumultuous battle near which stood hosts of Siddhas and soldiers, as arrows with downward-pointed and upward-pointed feathers— terrible to behold like Garuḍas and venomous serpents— rained down upon them.

Vāsava was unable to extinguish that abode of unbearable splendor with showers of weapons discharged in continuous succession, just as a cloud cannot extinguish with its own waters the fire that has fallen from within it.
Then, from his forearm marked with yellow sandalwood paste,
Raghu severed the bowstring of Indra with a crescent-headed arrow that emitted a deep sound like the churning ocean.
Casting aside his bow, his envy having grown intense,
he took up a weapon that was radiant with a shimmering halo and capable of stripping the wings from mountains, in order to exile his powerful adversary.
Struck violently in the chest by him, Raghu fell to the ground along with the tears of his soldiers;
yet, having shaken off the pain in a mere moment, he rose up together with the shouts of joy from the troops.

Nevertheless, the slayer of Vṛtra was gratified by the extraordinary prowess of him who remained steadfast even while his enemies were intent on cruel acts of weaponry; for a position is established everywhere by means of virtues.
"Even among the mountains, my weapon has never been withstood by anyone other than you because of its inherent strength;
know that I am pleased, and choose a boon, with the exception of my horse," the slayer of Vṛtra said to him.

Then, withdrawing the arrow— which had been drawn from the quiver but not fully released, its golden-feathered shaft coloring his fingers— the son of Dilīpa, speaking kindly, replied to the Lord of the Gods.
If my lord deems it right that the horse not be released,
then let my preceptor— whose body has been consecrated by continuous initiation— be endowed today with the entire fruit of the sacrifice, as if the ritual were completed according to the rules.
O Lord of Heaven, since you are a portion of the Three-eyed God (Śiva) and thus difficult to approach,
let it be so arranged that the lord of the people, seated in his assembly hall, hears this account from you alone through the messenger of your message.

Having assented to Rāghava’s request with the words "So be it," Mātali, whose chariot he drove, departed as he had come; and the son of Sudakṣiṇā, his mind not entirely cheerful, also returned to the king’s assembly hall.
The Lord of Creatures, first awakened by the messenger of Hari,
greeted him while stroking his body— marked with the scars of the thunderbolt— with a hand trembling with joy.
Thus the lord of the earth, whose commands were honored, having performed ninety-nine great sacrifices,
stretched them out like a flight of stairs as he desired to ascend to heaven at the end of his life.

Then he, his soul withdrawn from the objects of the senses, having duly bestowed the white sunshade—the emblem of sovereignty—upon his young son, took refuge with that queen in the shade of the trees of a sage’s grove; for this is the family vow of the Ikṣvākus when their age has faded.
Thus ends the third canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
Having accepted the kingdom bestowed by his father, he shone even more brightly,
like the sacrificial fire when the light of the sun has been transferred to it at the end of the day.
And for those kings who heard that Dilīpa had laid down his weapons and become their sovereign,
it was as if a stake of anguish were driven into their hearts from which all arrows had been extracted.
Like the rows of banners on Indra’s standard,
the subjects, along with their children, rejoiced at the sight of his new accession to power.
Simultaneously, he who moved with the gait of an elephant ascended both his father’s lion throne and the entire circle of his enemies.
It is said that Padmā herself, remaining invisible, attended upon him who was consecrated for imperial sovereignty, using her own shadow as a visible canopy of lotuses.
And whenever those who were to be saluted approached at various times,
Sarasvatī attended upon that one worthy of praise with meaningful hymns of praise, as if through her own presence.
Although the earth had been enjoyed by venerable kings beginning with Manu, nevertheless, it seemed as if it had never belonged to anyone else before him.
For he won the hearts of the entire world by his judicious administration of justice, just as the southern breeze, being neither too cold nor too hot, wins the hearts of all.
Granted that her eyes resembled the petals of a lotus,
yet true sight comes through the scripture, which reveals the meaning of subtle matters.
Just as the moon is so called because it gladdens, and the sun because it heats,
even so did that king become true to his name by pleasing the subjects.
Those skilled in statecraft presented both the right and the wrong courses to the new king;
yet only the former position prevailed with him, while the latter found no place.
Because of his superior virtues toward his elder, he caused the people’s longing for him to diminish,
just as the fruit of a mango tree causes its blossoms to fade.
The qualities of even the five elements attained excellence;
under that new protector of the earth, everything seemed as if it were new once more.
Then, royal fortune— characterized by autumnal lotuses— approached him who was established in well-being through the pacification of his afflictions, like a second Śarad herself.
With the clouds having shed their rain and become light, the quarters of the sky expanded for both him and the sun, as if they were yielded up for his majesty.
Thinking, "This is the time for Raghu to string his weapon," Indra,
as if apprehensive, withdrew his own bow.
The season, with its white lotuses as parasols and blooming kāśa grass as fly-whisks, imitated him; yet it did not attain his splendor.
At that moment, the delight of those with sight was equal toward both of them: toward him, whose face was bright with serenity, and toward the moon, whose radiance was clear.
Upon the rows of swans, upon the stars, and upon the waters filled with white lotuses,
the glories of his subjects were scattered as if they were his own fame.
Seated in the shade of sugarcane, the women guarding the rice fields sang of the fame of that protector,
extolling the excellence of his virtues from the time of his childhood onwards.
At the rising of the great-spirited Kumbhayoni, the waters became clear;
yet at the rise of Raghu, the minds of his enemies, fearing defeat, were agitated.
Great bulls, fierce with rut, humped, and tearing up the banks of rivers,
encountered his prowess with playful ease.
Struck by the blossoms of the *saptaparṇa* trees, fragrant with ichor,
those elephants exuded [ichor] from seven parts of their bodies as if out of envy.
Making the rivers fordable and the roads free from sticky mud,
the autumn season first urged him toward his expedition by means of its favorable power.
To him, the fire, properly fed with oblations during the rite of the *vājinīrājanā*,
bestowed victory as if with a hand in the guise of its clockwise-turning flames.
With his frontiers and rear-guard well-protected, his flanks pure,
and endowed with speed, he set out, taking with him the sixfold army, desiring to conquer the quarters.
The city women, advanced in years, scattered parched grain over him,
just as the waves of the milk-ocean, tossed by Mount Mandara, showered droplets upon Acyuta.
Equal to Prācīnabarhis, he first set out toward the east,
as if threatening his enemies with banners fluttering in the wind.
Making the sky appear like the surface of the earth with the dust raised by his chariots, and making the surface of the earth appear like the sky with his elephants resembling clouds; Ragh(K)_4.29 //
First came his majesty, then the sound of his chariot, followed by the vanguard;
last of all went the elephant division—thus that army marched as if it were composed of four columns.
The rivers along his path were made turbid by those who preceded him, shallow by those who traveled with him, and muddy by those who followed behind.
By virtue of his power, he rendered the mountain ridges waterless, the navigable rivers easy to cross, and the forests bright with light.
Leading that vast army toward the eastern ocean,
he shone like Bhagīratha leading the Gaṅgā as it fell from the matted locks of Śiva.
With kings deprived of their fruit, uprooted, and broken in many ways,
his path was made prominent by them, just as that of an elephant is by trees.
Thus traversing various eastern regions as he conquered them,
he reached the shore of the great ocean, dark with groves of palm trees.
Therefore, from that one who uproots those who are not submissive, as if from the current of a river,
the Suhmas protected themselves by adopting the behavior of a reed.
Having swiftly uprooted the Vaṅgas, who were arrogant in their naval forces,
that leader erected pillars of victory within the channels of the Ganges' current.
Bowing down at his lotus feet, they, like *kalamā* rice plants uprooted and replanted, caused Raghu to flourish with their fruits.
Having crossed the Kāverī with his troops by means of bridges formed from bound elephants,
he proceeded toward Kaliṅga, guided along the path by the people of Utkala.
He fixed his sharp prowess upon the head of Mahendra,
just as a driver fixes a goad upon the head of a deep-sensing elephant.
The King of Kaliṅga, whose force was his elephants, countered him with missiles,
just as a mountain raining down stones opposes Indra when he is intent on clipping its wings.
Having endured there that downpour of iron arrows from his enemies, the descendant of Kakutstha attained the glory of victory as if he had bathed in an auspicious rite.
From the elephant division shaken by the Vāyavya weapon, as if from the ocean churned by its wings,
he seized the Kalinga king like Tārkṣya seizing a serpent.
Having prepared their drinking grounds with the leaves of betel vines,
his warriors drank coconut liquor as well as the fame of their enemies.
That king, victorious through righteousness, having captured and then released [the enemy],
took away the modesty of the lord of the great Indra, but not his land.
Then, along the very shore of the sea, which was adorned with rows of fruit-bearing betel-nut trees,
he marched toward the quarter frequented by Agastya, intent on achieving invincible victory.
By the enjoyment of his army, fragrant with the ichor of elephants,
he made the Kāverī seem as if it were a rival wife to the lord of rivers, the ocean.
By him, the dust of the army was made to serve as a substitute for scented powder upon the tresses of the Kerala women, who had cast off their ornaments out of fear.
The foothills of the Malaya mountain, where black pepper was left behind by the harītas birds, were occupied by the forces of that king as he proceeded on his journey of conquest.
The dust arising from the fields of ripe paddy trampled by the hooves of well-bred horses suddenly pervaded the sky, which was already turbid with the cocoons of insects.

The neck-chains of the elephants, though they tore through their foot-tethers, did not slip off as they moved along the paths encircled by the coils of serpents, for they were fastened with sandalwood.
In that very southern quarter, even the splendor of the sun grows dim;
there, the Pāṇḍyas could not endure the majesty of Raghu.
Having descended, they presented to him the finest pearls from the great ocean where it meets the Tāmraparṇī river,
as if offering their own accumulated glory.
Having enjoyed himself as he desired upon those two mountains, Malaya and Dardura— which had sandalwood trees growing at their slopes— he beheld them like the breasts of that very quarter of the sky.
He of irresistible prowess crossed the Sahya mountain, which had been left far behind by the ocean and resembled the slope of the earth with its garment of fallen clouds.
By his advancing armies, intent on conquering the western regions,
even though Rāma was driven away, he remained as if clinging to the Sahya mountains like the ocean.
The kaitaka pollen, which had previously been blown ahead by the wind,
became the effortless perfuming powder for the turbans of the warriors.
The rustling of his mounts and chariots surpassed the sound of groves of royal palm trees shaken by the wind.
From the *punnāga* trees, bees fell upon the temples of the elephants— temples bound with the trunks of date palms and fragrant with the outpouring of ichor.
It is said that the Ocean, being entreated by Rāma, granted him space;
under the pretext of being the king of the western borderlands, he paid tribute to the descendant of Raghu.
There, he made Mount Trikūṭa itself a lofty pillar of victory, its distinct marks of prowess carved by the tusks of his great elephants.
Then he set out by a land route to conquer the Persians,
just as a self-controlled ascetic sets out with the knowledge of reality to conquer his enemies known as the senses.
He could not endure the intoxication of the wine from the lotus-faces of the Yavana women,
just as the unseasonable rising of clouds cannot endure the morning sunlight upon the lotuses.
A tumultuous battle ensued between him and the cavalry of the Persians;
amidst the dust, the opposing combatants could only be identified by the twang of their Śārṅga bows.
With their bearded heads severed by his arrows,
he covered the earth as if with honeycombs swarming with bees.
The remaining ones, having removed their helmets, sought refuge with him;
for the wrath of great-souled beings is appeased by prostration.
Those warriors dispelled the fatigue of their victory with honey-wines upon the grounds of vineyards,
where precious deer-skins were spread out.
Then Raghu set out toward the northern quarter like the sun,
intending to extract the northern regions with his arrows as the sun draws up moisture with its rays.
Having made those very conquerors his precursors on the chariots, he, unconquerable himself,
entered the northern region like the submarine fire entering the great ocean.
Their fatigue from the journey relieved by rolling along the banks of the Vaṅkṣu,
his horses shook their manes, which were entangled with saffron filaments.
There, the deeds of Raghu toward the husbands of the Hun women displayed manifest valor, serving as an instruction for splitting their cheeks.
The Kambojas were unable to withstand his prowess in battle;
they were brought low along with the acorns crushed by the feet of elephants weary from tethering posts.
Masses of lofty wealth, consisting mostly of excellent horses,
entered that lord of the people as rivers flow into the ocean.
Then, accompanied by his retinue, he ascended the mountain that is the father of Gaurī,
as if increasing its peaks with the rising dust of its minerals.
He praised those of equal courage for their lack of agitation even amidst the roar of the army,
like lions dwelling in caves who turn back to look around.
On the way, the breezes attended upon him— breezes that rustled the birch leaves, caused the whistling sound of the hollow bamboos, and bore the spray of the Gaṅgā.
The soldiers rested,
taking shelter in the shade of *nameru* trees upon rocks whose surfaces were scented by the musk of deer reclining thereon.
At night, the medicinal herbs growing near the leader [of the army], their brilliance enhanced by the neck-chains of the elephants tethered to the *sarala* trees,
served as lamps without oil.
In his dwellings, the deodar trees, by their rubbing against the temples of elephants moistened with rut-fluid,
indicated to the Kirātas that they were the bodies of noble elephants.
There, a fierce conflict took place with those mountaineers,
in which fire burst forth from the clashing of iron arrows, slings, and stones.
Having made the Utsavasanketas pay tribute with his arrows,
that successful king had the Kinnaras sing the praises of the victory of his arms.
As they stood before one another with offerings in their hands,
the King was recognized as the essence of the Himalayas, and the Himalayan mountain as the essence of the King.
There, having established Akṣobhya as a mass of glory,
he descended from the mountain that had been rivalled by the descendant of Pulastya, as if taking away its shame.
When he had crossed the Lauhitya, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa trembled along with the black aloe-wood trees that served as the tethering posts for his elephants.
He could not even endure the dust raised by the rows of chariots, which obscured the sun and created a cloudless yet gloomy day; how much less could he withstand the army with its banners?

The Lord [of the earth] took as his own those elephants with split temples—possessing prowess exceeding that of Indra—who had been employed by others to restrain him; for he was the master of those who could assume any form at will.
The Lord of Kāmarūpa worshipped the shadow of his feet— the presiding deity of his golden throne— with an offering of jeweled flowers.
Having thus conquered the quarters, the Victorious One turned back, allowing the dust raised by his chariot to settle upon the crests of the kings' heads, now shorn of their umbrellas.
He performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, in which one's entire property is given as the sacrificial fee;
for the acquisitions of the virtuous are indeed for the sake of renunciation, just like the gathering of clouds by rain-givers.

At the conclusion of the sacrificial session, the descendant of Kakutstha, accompanied by his ministers, permitted the kings— whose resentment over their defeat had been assuaged by generous honors and whose wives were anxious due to their long separation— to return to their own cities.
With prostrations at his departure, they made the pair of feet of the emperor— marked with the signs of the line, the banner, the jar, and the parasol, and obtainable only through his grace—
yellowish-white with the pollen and nectar falling from the garlands on their crowns as they touched his toes.
Thus ends the fourth canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
To that lord of the earth at the Viśvajit sacrifice, who had bestowed his entire treasury without reserve,
Kautsa— the pupil of Varatantu— approached, having acquired knowledge and seeking the means for his teacher’s fee.

Having placed the guest-offering in an earthen vessel because he had discarded all that was made of gold, the king— whose virtue was beyond price, who was radiant with fame, and who was hospitable by nature— went out to meet his guest, whose splendor was illuminated by sacred learning.

Having honored that ascetic according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the people— who was skilled in discerning what ought to be done, foremost among those whose wealth is honor, and knowledgeable in ritual— joined his palms in reverence and addressed the one seated upon the seat.
O you of keen intellect, is your preceptor well— he who is the foremost among the seers who composed the mantras—
since from him you have obtained all knowledge, just as one initiated by Ugra obtains consciousness?

I hope that the threefold austerity of the Great Sage— performed through body, speech, and mind— is not being brought to ruin by obstacles, which would cause a lapse in the fortitude of even Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.

I hope that no calamity from wind or other elements has befallen those trees of the hermitage— which dispel fatigue and have been nurtivated with efforts such as providing foundations and binding, and which are indistinguishable from your own sons?

Out of affection even for those things used for ritual purposes, the sages have not thwarted the desires of the deer; thus, I hope the birth of the does remains unblemished, as their umbilical cords fall off while they lie upon the sacrificial grass in their laps.

I trust that those auspicious waters of the sacred fords— by which the ritual ablutions of initiation are performed and from which the handfuls of funeral offerings are cast for the ancestors— are present for you, their sandy banks marked by the gleanings of the sixth part?

I hope that the forest produce which serves as the means for maintaining your bodies— such as the ripening wild rice and other grains— is accepted by the country folk even from their fodder, and that it is shared with guests who arrive at the proper time.
Has the great seer, being well-pleased, permitted you to return home after having properly instructed you?
For now is the time for you to proceed to the second stage of life, which is capable of benefiting all.
My mind is not satiated by merely visiting you, O Arhat; it is eager to perform service for you.
Whether by the command of your teacher or of your own accord, you have come from the forest to honor me.
Having heard Raghu’s noble speech regarding the cow, even though Kautsa had inferred the king’s vast wealth from the vessel for the guest-offering,
he replied to that blameless monarch with his hopes for his own purpose now weakened.
"Know, O King, that all is well with us; for while you are our protector, how could misfortune befall your subjects?
When the sun is shining, how could darkness serve to obstruct the vision of the world?"

Devotion toward those worthy of honor is appropriate for your lineage; by your great magnanimity, you have surpassed your ancestors. It is my sorrow that I have come to you as a petitioner only now, after the proper time has passed.
O lord of men, standing there with only your body remaining, you shine with the splendor bestowed by sacred fords;
you resemble a stalk of wild rice left behind, its fruit and ears having been gathered by forest-dwellers.
It is fitting that you, being the sole lord of men, manifest this state of possessing nothing born of sacrifice;
for the waning of the digits of the moon, after it has been drunk in turn by the gods, is indeed more praiseworthy than its waxing.
Therefore, since I have no other duty, I shall strive to procure the teacher’s fee from elsewhere.
May it be well with you; for even the *cātaka* bird does not distress an autumnal cloud whose interior has already shed its water.

Having said this much, the king restrained the disciple of the great seer who was desiring to depart, and questioned him: "O wise one, what object should be given by you to the teacher, and how much is it?"
Then that wise student explained the matter at hand to him— the teacher of the castes and stages of life— who had performed the sacrifice according to rule and was free from the influence of pride.
Having acquired knowledge, I requested the great seer for a teacher’s fee;
he, however, regarded my long-standing and unswerving devotion as being more significant than that.
Then, his anger having been aroused by my persistence, my teacher, disregarding my emaciation, said to me:
"Bring me fourteen crores of wealth, corresponding to the number of sciences you have mastered."
Therefore, perceiving you to be one whose title of "Lord" remains only in name, I now venture not to detain you with the implements for the rites of hospitality,
for my debt for the sacred learning [I have received] is no small matter.
Thus addressed by the twice-born, the best among those who know the Vedas,
he who possessed the splendor of the moon and whose sensory functions were turned away from sin, the sole lord of the world spoke further to him.
May this new ground for censure not arise against me: that one who was seeking wealth for his preceptor, who had mastered the Vedas, yet failed to obtain his desire from Raghu, went to another donor.

O worthy one, you who have been honored by me, you ought to endure two or three days while residing in my fire-sanctuary like a fourth sacred fire, until that which is prepared for your sake is accomplished.
Saying "So be it," the one of noble birth (Raghu), perceiving that promise to be infallible, accepted the agreement;
and Raghu, seeing that the earth had been stripped of its essence, desired to extract wealth from Kuvera.
Indeed, due to the power born from the sprinkling of Vasiṣṭha’s mantras, the movement of his chariot was not obstructed over the oceans, the sky, or the mountains,
just like that of a cloud accompanied by the wind.
Then at nightfall, the steadfast Raghu, purified in his vows, lay down upon the chariot prepared for him and filled with weapons;
he did so out of mere consideration for his feudatories, desiring to conquer the Lord of Kailāsa by sheer force.
In the morning, those appointed to report to him as he was about to set out on his journey announced with joyful wonder that a rain of gold had fallen from the sky into the middle of the treasury.
The king bestowed that entire heap of radiant gold, obtained from Kubera who was being assailed [by the gods],
upon Kautsa, just as one might give a portion of Mount Sumeru split by the thunderbolt.
To the people dwelling in Sāketa, both of them were objects of adoration:
the petitioner, who was free from desire for more than what was due to his preceptor, and the king, who bestowed even more than what the petitioner desired.

Then, his purpose accomplished by the gift of a hundred female camels and mares, the wise Kautsa, with a joyful heart, touched the lord of subjects—who stood with his body slightly bent—with his hand as he set forth, and spoke these words: *athoṣṭravāmīśatahāritārthaṃ prajeśvaraṃ prītamanā manīṣī / spṛśankareṇānatapūrvakāyaṃ samprasthito vākyamuvāca kautsaḥ //* Ragh(K)_5.32 // I have received my wealth from you, O Lord of Creatures; now I depart. May you be victorious over your enemies, and may your prosperity increase through the growth of your offspring. May the earth, filled with grain, yield its produce without labor, and may the gods grant you rain at the proper time. May the wind blow pleasantly for you, and may the sun shine with gentle heat. May the night be auspicious for you, and may the moon rise for your welfare. May the quarters of the sky be favorable to you, and may the planets move in harmony. May the seasons be agreeable to you, and may your days pass in happiness. May your nights be peaceful, and may your mornings bring you joy. May your midday be free from distress, and may your evening be serene. May your life be long, and may your fame endure. May your lineage be unbroken, and may your virtues be ever-increasing. May you be protected by the gods, and may you be blessed by the sages. May you be victorious in all your endeavors, and may you be prosperous in every way. May you be free from disease, and may you be endowed with health. May you be honored by your kin, and may you be respected by your subjects. May you be beloved by your friends, and may you be trusted by your allies. May you be firm in your resolve, and may you be steady in your conduct. May you be wise in your counsel, and may you be brave in your deeds. May you be generous in your giving, and may you be humble in your heart. May you be patient in adversity, and may you be joyful in prosperity. May you be constant in your devotion, and may you be steadfast in your dharma. May you be vigilant in your duties, and may you be mindful of your goals. May you be compassionate toward all beings, and may you be impartial in your justice. May you be self-controlled in your senses, and may you be disciplined in your mind. May you be enlightened in your wisdom, and may you be liberated in your soul. May you attain the highest state, and may you reach the ultimate goal. May you be blessed with peace, and may you be established in bliss. May you be free from all obstacles, and may you be successful in all your aims. May you be protected by the guardians of the world, and may you be favored by the lords of the quarters. May you be shielded by the mountains, and may you be sustained by the oceans. May you be supported by the earth, and may you be upheld by the heavens. May you be guided by the stars, and may you be illuminated by the light of knowledge. May you be purified by your austerities, and may you be sanctified by your sacrifices. May you be adorned by your virtues, and may you be graced by your merits. May you be crowned with success, and may you be anointed with prosperity. May you be exalted in honor, and may you be elevated in status. May you be renowned for your glory, and may you be celebrated for your fame. May you be praised by the virtuous, and may you be honored by the wise. May you be revered by the elders, and may you be esteemed by the learned. May you be beloved by the young, and may you be respected by the old. May you be a refuge for the distressed, and may you be a protector for the helpless. May you be a guide for the lost, and may you be a leader for the followers. May you be a teacher for the ignorant, and may you be a friend for the seekers. May you be a father to the children, and may you be a mother to the weak. May you be a brother to the lonely, and may you be a companion to the weary. May you be a kinsman to the stranger, and may you be a relative to the orphan. May you be a benefactor to the needy, and may you be a sustainer of the poor. May you be a giver of hope to the despondent, and may you be a source of comfort to the grieving. May you be a beacon for the wandering, and may you be a haven for the wayfarer. May you
What is surprising in this, that the earth yields all desires for a sovereign of his subjects who abides by the path of righteousness?
But your power is inconceivable, by which even the sky was milked according to your wish.
For you who have attained all blessings, any further wish would be a mere redundancy;
may you obtain a son worthy of your own virtues, just as your venerable father was to you.
Having thus offered his benediction, the foremost of beings returned to the presence of his preceptor;
the king, for his part, quickly obtained a son from him, just as the world of living beings receives light from the sun.
It is said that during the *brāhma* hour, his queen gave birth to a son who was like a young Kumāra;
therefore, his father named that first-born son Aja after Brahmā himself.
The prince’s form was as majestic, his vigor was the same, and his natural loftiness was identical;
he did not differ from his progenitor, just as a lamp lit from another lamp does not differ from it.

Although the Goddess Śrī desired him— who had duly acquired knowledge from his teachers and was made exceptionally beautiful by the blossoming of youth— she awaited her father’s permission, just as a steadfast maiden awaits her father’s consent when she longs for a husband.
Then, King Bhoja of the Krathakaiśikas, eager to bring his nephew for the sake of Indumatī’s svayaṃvara,
dispatched a trusted messenger to Raghu.
Reflecting upon that praiseworthy alliance and considering his son to have reached the stage suitable for marriage,
he dispatched him with an army to the prosperous capital of the Lord of Vidarbha.

For the son of the lord of men, the halting places along the road— wherein hospitality was prepared in the guest-houses and which were not barren of the offerings of the local people— became like pleasure-gardens for recreation.

Having traversed the road, he encamped his army— whose horses from the forest of Āyodhyā were frothing with fatigue— on the bank of the Narmadā, where the rows of banners were made to dance by breezes moist with spray.
Then, from above, a wild elephant emerged from the river— its entry into the water previously signaled by bees hovering over it, its broad temples washed clean of rut.
On the slopes of Ṛkṣavān,
he indicated the traces of his passage by means of two teeth, which were blunted against rocks and mottled with dark, upward-streaked lines of red chalk washed down by the floodwaters.
With a hand capable of swift withdrawal and extension, he shone as he suddenly broke the waves facing the shore with a sound, like one who has begun to break through the bolts of water.

Expert in swimming, he moved along the bank, dragging with him the soft shoots of *kāraṇḍava* reeds left over from the bathing of Pulinda women— their girdles— and the mossy creepers clinging to the water's edge.
The splendor of the rutting-fluid, which had been momentarily stilled on the temples of that solitary elephant as he plunged into the lake,
blazed forth again at the sight of other wild elephants.
Having inhaled his unbearable rut, which flowed with the pungent milk of seven-leaved trees,
the lordly elephants of the army turned away, disregarding the strenuous efforts of their drivers.

In an instant, he threw that military camp into a tumultuous state: its yokes were severed and its draft animals fled, leaving it empty; its chariots had broken axles or were overturned; and its warriors were distracted by the need to rescue their women.
Hearing that the wild elephant was not to be slain by the king as it charged toward him, the prince,
wishing to turn it back, struck it on the forehead with an arrow from his bowstring drawn neither too far nor too short.
As soon as he was pierced, it is said that he cast off his serpent form; watched by the astonished army, he assumed a beautiful celestial body standing in the midst of a shimmering halo of light.
Then, having showered the prince with flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling trees that had appeared through his supernatural power,
the eloquent sage spoke, the pearl necklace upon his chest enhanced by the radiance of his teeth.
"Know me to be Priyamvada, the son of Priyadarshana, the lord of the Gandharvas; due to the arrogance rooted in pride, I incurred the curse of Matanga and attained the state of a wild elephant."
And after I had subsequently entreated that great seer with prostrations, he became gentle;
for while heat arises from contact with fire and sunlight, coolness is indeed the natural state of water.
"When Aja, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, shall break your jar with an iron-tipped arrow,
you will be reunited with your own majesty"— thus did that treasure-house of asceticism speak to me.
I have been liberated from the power of the curse by you and have attained the destiny ordained by the Creator;
for if I were not to perform a service for you in return, my recovery of my own status would indeed be in vain.
Therefore, accept from me this Gandharva weapon, whose mantras for employment and withdrawal are distinct;
it is called Prasvāpana, by which the striker gains victory while causing no harm to his enemies.
Enough of this shame toward me, since even while striking me you were for a moment intent on compassion;
therefore, when I am seeking to persuade you, you should not employ the harshness of refusal.
Saying "So be it," that moon among men, having sipped the purifying water of the river born from the Moon,
and facing northward, received from him the mantra for the weapon, being one who had mastered the science of missiles and was firm in his resolve.
