Thus, as they traveled along the road, a friendship arose between them by the turn of fate for reasons beyond imagining;
one went toward the regions of Caitraratha, delightful due to their excellent governance, while the other proceeded to Vidarbha.
As he stood near the outskirts of the city, the King of Krathakaiśika— filled with a profound joy born from the arrival of that guest—
went out to meet him, like the ocean with its surging waves approaching the moon.
Having led him into the city, the leader, whose splendor was enhanced by his humility,
attended upon him with such reverence that all the people gathered there believed the prince of Vidarbha had come to the house of Aja as a guest.

Pointed out by his bowing officials, that representative of Raghu ascended the beautiful new palace, where golden jars were placed at the front entrance upon the altar; it was as if the God of Love had entered the stage of life immediately following childhood.
There, for Aja— who desired that lovely jewel of a maiden before whom the assembly of kings had gathered at her *svayaṃvara*—
sleep, turbid with the awakening of his passion, finally turned toward his eyes like a beloved woman at night.

At dawn, bards awakened him—who resembled the rising sun—with words charming through their graceful composition; he whose thick shoulders were pressed by his ear-ornaments and whose body-unguents were thinned by friction against the bedspread.
The night has passed, O best of the wise; leave your bed. Surely the burden of the world was divided into two parts by the Creator:
that which your father bears with unwearied effort, and that upon which you stand as the support for his other shoulder.
Overcome by sleep, you indeed fail to look upon her; thus, like a woman distressed when her lover has departed, the goddess Lakṣmī passes the night in longing.
Even that moon, hanging at the edge of the horizon, loses its splendor before the radiance of your face as it seeks diversion.
By that simultaneous opening of your lovely eyes, let these two immediately attain mutual likeness:
your eye, with its pupil quivering and soft within, and the lotus, with its bee moving inside.
The morning breeze loosens the flowers from the stalks of the trees and mingles with the lotuses opened by the rays of the sun;
it seems to desire for your breath the natural fragrance that belongs to another.
The snowy water, fallen upon copper-red tree shoots and bright as a polished pearl from a necklace,
appears like your smile— intermingled with the moonlight of your teeth and enhanced by the luster of your bimba-red lips.
Before the sun, the treasury of heat, can assail the world, darkness has already been dispelled by Aruṇa;
for when you, O hero, have gone to the vanguard of battle, why indeed would your father himself destroy the enemies?
Those army elephants, whose sleep has been dispelled by both flanks, leave their beds while dragging their clanging chains;
their tusks shine with the hue of the young dawn, appearing like the slopes of a mountain split open to reveal the red ochre within.
O lotus-eyed one, these steeds from Vanāyu, restrained within long cloth pavilions, have shaken off their sleep;
now, as they stand before us, these draft animals warm the pieces of rock-salt intended for licking with the heat of their breath.
Devotion has become sparse, the offering of flowers withered, and the lamps are devoid of the radiance of their surrounding halos;
even this sweet-voiced parrot of yours in its cage repeats our words intended to awaken you.

Thus, having dispelled his sleep, that broad-shouldered prince, like the elephant Supratīka on the sandy banks of the Ganges, left his bed while the women of his retinue were busy at his feet; the ends of the coverlet were caught by the jewels of their bracelets.

Then, having completed the rites prescribed by the scriptures that were appropriate for the commencement of the day, he— whose eyelashes were curved and whose attire was suitably arranged by skilled artisans— went to the assembly of kings gathered for the svayaṃvara.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.

There he beheld kings seated upon thrones on couches resembling celestial palaces, their physical splendor intensified as if by the power of a kalpa; they appeared like sacrificial posts erected upon golden altars.

As the kings gazed upon the descendant of Kakutstha— who, as it were, had his own body surrendered to him by the Lord (Śiva) through the favor he had previously received— their hearts became hopeless regarding Indumatī.
Then the prince ascended the dais pointed out by Vaidarbha by means of the constructed flight of steps,
just as a young lion cub climbs a lofty mountain ridge by means of rocky ledges.
Seated upon a jewel-studded throne covered with a spread of the finest color,
he possessed a splendor that was most comparable to that of Guha when he rested upon the back of a peacock.

In those royal successions, resplendent with glory, he shone as his self divided into a thousand forms— difficult to behold due to the arising of such extraordinary luster— just as lightning flashes within rows of clouds.
In their midst— those who were seated upon costly thrones and arrayed in magnificent attire—
the son of Raghu alone shone with his own splendor, like the Pārijāta tree among the Kalpavṛkṣas.
The rows of eyes of the city folk fell upon him, leaving all other kings behind,
like wild bees deserting flowering trees when a scent-elephant, intoxicated with rut, enters their domain.

When the conch shells were blown and the sound of musical instruments, intended for auspicious purposes, swelled toward the horizons on all sides, it became the cause for the peacocks dwelling in the groves near the city to perform their spirited dances.

Mounted upon a four-sided palanquin carried by men, adorned by her retinue of maidens, and dressed in garments mixed with festive ornaments, the maiden who was to choose a husband entered the royal highway between the rows of platforms.
At that extraordinary creation of the Creator, consisting of a maiden and the object of a thousand eyes,
the lords of men fell with their inner hearts, while their bodies remained merely upon their seats.

Various amorous gestures arose from those kings whose desires were clearly manifested toward her; they served as the foremost messengers of their affection, like the beauty of swaying branches on trees stirred by a gentle breeze.
With both hands he whirled a play-lotus, its stalk embraced by his palms, which struck the bees with its trembling petals and was beautified by a halo of pollen within.

Another graceful man, turning his handsome face slightly to one side, lifted the cloak that had slipped from his shoulder and— having momentarily caught it on the tip of his armlet— returned it to its proper place.
Then another, with the tips of his fingers slightly curled and the beauty of his eyes somewhat cast down,
scratched the golden footstool with a foot whose nail-lustre was mingled with the rays of gems.
Another, having placed his left arm— adorned with a heavy bracelet— at the edge of the seat by pressing it against his side,
became intent on conversing with a friend, his necklace displaced as his hips were turned.
Another youth tore with the tips of his fingernails— a ketaka petal as pale as the ivory ear-ornament of a wanton woman— the very mark left upon it by contact with the hips of his beloved.
With a hand whose palm was as copper-red as a lotus and marked with the sign of a banner,
he gracefully cast the dice, which were illuminated by the radiance of his shining finger-rings.
Someone else, though remaining in his assigned place, seemed as if he had overstepped his own station;
he applied one hand, with its fingers encased in rays of diamonds, to his crown.
Then Sunandā, the guardian of the inner apartments, who was as eloquent as a man and well-versed in the learning, conduct, and lineages of kings,
led the princess into the presence of the Lord of Magadha and spoke to her.

He was a refuge for those seeking protection, possessed of unfathomable courage, established in Magadha, and a king who had won renown by pleasing his subjects; he was named Parantapa, a name that accorded perfectly with his deeds.
Granted that there may be kings numbering in the thousands, yet they say this earth possesses a true king because of him;
for though a night is crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, it is radiant only through the moon.
Through the continuous performance of sacrifices, he— whose thousand eyes were constantly summoned—
long deprived Śacī of her tresses, which hung down over her pale cheeks and were once adorned with mandāra flowers.
If you desire that his hand be taken by this most excellent groom during his entrance,
then cause him to become a festival for the eyes of the women of Puṣpapura as they lean from the windows of the palaces.

When she had spoken thus, the slender maiden, her garland of madhūka flowers and dūrvā grass slightly loosened as she looked at him, rebuked him by means of a simple gesture of salutation alone, without uttering a word.
Then, the woman appointed to carry the cane led the princess to another king,
just as a line of waves stirred by the wind leads a royal swan from one lotus to another in Lake Mānasa.

And this lord of men, whose youthful splendor was coveted by celestial nymphs and who, according to the authors of the Sūtras, occupies the portion of humility, spoke to her: "Even while remaining on earth, he enjoys the status of Indra."
By shedding teardrops as large as pearls upon their breasts,
he provided necklaces for the wives of his enemies' foes without even the string to fasten them.
In this world, Fortune and Sarasvatī—whose natural abodes are distinct—dwell together in one place;
O auspicious lady, you alone, by virtue of your beauty, your speech, and your truthfulness, are a worthy third to them both.
Then, withdrawing her gaze from the King of Aṅga, the princess said to her companions, "Let us go.
It was not that he was undesirable, nor that she did not know how to see him properly; rather, the world has diverse tastes.
Thereafter, the female doorkeeper stationed at the entrance presented to him the king, who was difficult for others to withstand and exceptionally handsome,
just as Indumatī showed him the newly risen moon.
This lord of Avanti, with his uplifted arms, broad chest, and slender, rounded waist,
shines like the sun having been mounted upon a lathe and carved by Tvaṣṭṛ using the whirling motion of a wheel.
In his expeditions, the dust raised by the leading horses of that king of complete power causes the setting of the sprouts of radiance from the crest-jewels of the subordinate vassals.
Dwelling not far from the abode of Mahākāla, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon,
he enjoys the pleasures of touch with his female companions even during the day through the moonlight filtering through the lattice windows.

O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps find pleasure in your heart in spending time with this young prince amidst the succession of gardens shaken by the breezes from the waves of the Siprā?
Even toward that reflection of light, which had dried up the mire of her enemies with its splendor,
she— possessing unsurpassed delicacy— did not fix her affection, just as the night-lotus does not feel passion for the sun.

Having placed before her that fair-featured Sunandā—who shone like the interior of a lotus and was not inferior in virtues to the king of Anūpa—the Creator fashioned a graceful creation; then Sunandā spoke once more.
It is said that the yogi Kārtavīrya possessed a thousand arms won in battle, had erected sacrificial posts throughout the eighteen islands,
and held the title of "King" which was not shared by any other.
Appearing before him at the very moment he thought of improper action,
the wielder of the bow— the discipliner who restrains the lack of discipline even within the bodies of living beings— gave his command.
In his prison, Daśānana— having conquered Vāsava— dwelt until [Rāma’s] favor was obtained, his arms rendered motionless by the binding of the bowstring and his rows of mouths sighing incessantly.
In his lineage was born this king named Pradīpa, a servant of the elders learned in the scriptures,
by whom the ill repute that the Goddess of Fortune is "naturally fickle" and thus prone to the fault of being unsteady in her resort has been wiped away.

Having obtained as his ally in battle the one whose path is black (Kṛṣṇa), he regards the sharp edge of Rāma’s axe— the night of destruction for the Kṣatriyas— as having the strength of a lotus petal.

O you whose beauty is like that of the digit of the moon, become the consort of this long-armed king if you have the desire to behold the river Revā, which is as beautiful as a braid of water and has the embankments of Māhiṣmatī for its girdle, visible through the lattice-windows of the palaces.
Although his appearance was exceedingly pleasing, that lord of the earth did not please her,
just as the full moon, its dark spots wiped away by the autumn season, does not delight the lotus when it is free from the cloud's shadow.

The maiden was addressed by the female guardian of the inner apartments regarding Suṣeṇa, the lord of the Śūrasenas, whose fame was sung in other lands and who was a lamp illuminating both lineages through their purity of conduct.

This king is of the Nīpa lineage and a performer of sacrifices; by relying upon his virtues, even natural enmity was cast aside by [his subjects] among themselves, as if they had entered the peaceful hermitage of the Siddhas.
In his own body, there was a splendor as delightful to the eyes as that of the moon;
yet in the palaces of his enemies, his unbearable brilliance blazed even through the sprouts of grass grown upon the rooftops of their mansions.
At the time of his water-sports, because of the washing away of the sandalwood paste from the breasts of the women in his harem,
the Yamunā— even though she had reached Mathurā— shone as if her waters were mingled with the waves of the Gaṅgā.
Having been saved from Tārkṣya by Kāliya, the dweller of the Yamunā, he wears the jewel surrendered by him, which,
with its luster spreading across his chest, puts to shame Kṛṣṇa along with his Kaustubha gem.
O beautiful one, having won this youthful husband, may you enjoy the splendor of your youth in Vṛndāvana— a place not inferior to Caitraratha— with a bed of soft sprouts topped by flowers.
And having occupied the stone slabs covered with *śaileya* and sprinkled with droplets of water,
behold the dance of peacocks in the lovely caves of Govardhana during the rainy season.
With her charming navel like a whirlpool, she— destined to become the wife of another— passed by that king as a river flowing toward the ocean passes a mountain encountered on its course.
Then, having approached the Lord of Kaliṅga named Hemāṅgada— whose arms were embraced by Aṅgada,
who had subdued the factions of his enemies, and whose face was like the young, full moon— a maidservant spoke to that youthful woman.
This lord of Mahendra and the great ocean, whose strength is equal to Mount Mahendra,
appears as if Mahendra himself were marching before him during his expeditions under the guise of the rutting elephants of his army.

That one of noble arms, the foremost of archers, bears upon the scars left by the bowstring two lines on his forearms that resemble the tracks of the captive Fortune of his enemies, as if moistened by tears mixed with collyrium.

From the latticed windows of his palace, Yama beheld the ocean, which, with its rows of palm trees upon the shore, awakens him as he sleeps— its deep roar putting to rest the drums that signal the end of the watches of the night.
Dwelling together with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees,
you shall have the drops of perspiration removed by breezes carrying the scent of clove blossoms brought from other islands.

Although thus awakened by her, the younger sister of the King of Vidarbha, whose form was so alluring, nevertheless turned away from him; she was like the Goddess of Fortune led away by human effort when fate is adverse.

Then a female door-keeper, approaching the lord of Nāgapura who was like a god in form, spoke to Bhojyā, who possessed the beauty of a Nāga woman: "O lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird, look this way! *Raghuvamśa* 6.59.
This Pāṇḍya king, with long necklaces resting upon his shoulders and his body anointed with yellow sandalwood paste,
shines like the king of mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and from which mountain torrents are gushing forth.

Agastya, the one who brought the great mountain Vindhya to a standstill and who drank and then released the lord of the oceans without remainder, becomes his personal priest for the ritual bath (*sausnātika*), out of affection for him whose body is still moist from the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice.
By him, who had obtained from Hara that weapon so difficult to acquire, the haughty Lord of Laṅkā,
fearing a future assault upon Janasthāna, once set out after forming an alliance for the sake of conquering Indra’s realm.

Now that you have been duly taken by the hand by this man of noble lineage, become the co-wife of the southern quarter— which has the ocean for its girdle and is studded with jewels— just as the heavy earth is wedded to him.

Be pleased to sport forever upon the plateaus of the Malaya mountains, where betel vines entwine with areca-nut trees, where sandalwood trees are embraced by cardamom creepers, and where the ground is strewn with the leaves of the *tamāla*.
This king has a body dark as the blue lotus, while you have a slender form fair as yellow pigment;
may your union be like that of lightning and a rain-cloud, for the mutual enhancement of your beauty.
That instruction of his found no entry into the heart of his father-in-law, the lord of Vidarbha,
just as a ray of the moon finds no place in a lotus that has closed its petals due to the sun’s disappearance.
Like the flickering flame of a lamp at night, as that maiden choosing her own husband passed by one after another,
each king fell into a state of pallor, like a turret on a royal highway.
When she appeared before him, the son of Raghu was overwhelmed with doubt as to whether he should choose her or not;
but his right arm dispelled his uncertainty with the throbbing of its armlet-fastenings.
Having obtained him, whose every limb was faultless, the princess desisted from approaching any other;
for a swarm of bees, having reached a mango tree in full bloom, does not long for another tree.
Perceiving that Indumatī, whose radiance was like the moon, had fixed her mental faculties entirely upon him,
Sunandā, who knew the proper sequence of events, began to speak these words at great length.
A scion of the Ikṣvāku lineage and the preeminent peak among kings, he was known as Kakutstha, endowed with all auspicious marks;
from him the lords of Uttarakosala, their aspirations lofty, have borne the praiseworthy title of Kākutstha.
Mounting Mahendra in the form of a great bull,
he who had assumed the playfulness of Pinākin in battle rendered the cheeks of the asura women devoid of decorative leaf-designs with his arrows.

He who, rubbing his own armlet against the armlet of Indra as the latter approached in his own preeminent form, took his place upon half the throne of the breaker of mountains, loosened by the striking of Airāvaṇa.
Born in that family of Indukīrti was King Dilīpa, a lamp for his lineage,
who stopped short of the ninety-nine sacrifices in order to avoid provoking the envy of Śakra.

While he ruled the earth, even the wind did not disarrange the silken garments of proud women who had fallen asleep halfway to their pleasure gardens; so who would have ventured to reach out a hand to steal their ornaments?

His son, Rāghava, now rules his station; he is the performer of the great Viśvajit sacrifice, who reduced his vast wealth—accumulated by the submission of the four quarters—to nothing but the remains of an earthen vessel.
His fame— having ascended the mountains, crossed the oceans, entered the abode of serpents,
and risen to the heights— is such that it is impossible to measure its extent.
That prince, born after him like Jayanta born after Indra, the lord of heaven, is a youth who,
being capable and worthy of his station, bears the heavy ancestral yoke of the world as one who truly fits the burden.
By virtue of your lineage, your beauty, your youth, and those various qualities preeminent in discipline, choose him who is your equal; let this jewel be united with gold.
Then, at the conclusion of Sunandā’s speech, the princess, softening her shame,
welcomed the prince with a gaze pure with favor, as if with a garland of choice.
Because of her modesty, she was unable to express her bond of longing for that youth;
yet, through the visible bristling of her hair, it emerged from the slender frame of the lovely-haired maiden, piercing through her very being.
When the female attendant was thus joking with her friend, the Tathāgatā, the cane-bearer said, "Noble lady, let us go elsewhere. Then the bride looked at her with a frown of resentment.

With her thighs like the trunk of an elephant, she, whose complexion was fair as powdered sandalwood, fastened that string— white with powder— around the neck of the joy of the Raghus in its proper place, as if it were affection incarnate.
With that garland made of auspicious flowers hanging from his broad chest,
that most excellent man felt as if the younger sister of the King of Vidarbha had cast the noose of her arms around his neck.

"The moonlight has reached the moon; the daughter of Jahnu has descended into the ocean, her worthy match now free from clouds"—thus did the citizens there, delighted by the union of such equal virtues, speak with one voice, words that were harsh to the ears of rival kings.
On one side was the circle of kings with their excellent factions delighted, and on the other was the canopy;
at dawn, it was like a lake where the lotuses have blossomed while the beds of night-lilies have returned to sleep.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the great poem, the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
